question_text: For the first 6 seconds of its motion, a particle moving in a straight line has velocity given by $v = t^3 - 9t^2 + 24t\text{ ms}^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds.

subparts.stem: Find the acceleration function for the particle.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time: $a(t) = v'(t)$.
step_by_step: Apply the power rule to each term in $v(t) = t^3 - 9t^2 + 24t$.
Derivative of $t^3$ is $3t^2$, $-9t^2$ is $-18t$, and $24t$ is $24$.

subparts.stem: Find the greatest velocity of the particle in the first 6 seconds.

mark_breakdown.desc: Evaluating $v(t)$ at the local maximum and endpoints ($t = 0, 2, 6$)
Concluding greatest velocity is $36\text{ ms}^{-1}$ occurring at $t = 6$

subparts.solution:
The greatest velocity of the particle occurs when $\frac{dv}{dt} = a = 0$ or at endpoints:
$$3t^2 - 18t + 24 = 0$$
$$t^2 - 6t + 8 = 0$$
$$(t - 2)(t - 4) = 0$$
$$\therefore t = 2\text{ or } 4$$

From the sign diagram of $a$, there is a local maximum at $t = 2$.
Testing critical values and endpoints:
- At $t = 0$ (end point): $v = 0\text{ ms}^{-1}$
- At $t = 2$ (local maximum): $v = 2^3 - 9(2)^2 + 24(2) = 8 - 36 + 48 = 20\text{ ms}^{-1}$
- At $t = 6$ (end point): $v = 6^3 - 9(6)^2 + 24(6) = 216 - 324 + 144 = 36\text{ ms}^{-1}$

$\therefore$ the greatest velocity of the particle is $36\text{ ms}^{-1}$ which occurs at $t = 6\text{ seconds}$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The absolute maximum of a continuous function on a closed interval occurs at either a critical point (where $v'(t) = 0$) or at one of the endpoints of the interval.
step_by_step: Solve $a(t) = 0$ for $t \in [0, 6]$ to find critical points $t = 2$ and $t = 4$.
Identify $t = 2$ as a local maximum via sign change of $a(t)$.
Compare values: $0, 20, 36$. The greatest is $36$ at $t = 6$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting to test the endpoints of the interval, mistakenly assuming the local maximum at $t=2$ is the global maximum.

subparts.stem: At what times in the first 6 seconds is the speed of the particle decreasing?

mark_breakdown.desc: Stating that speed is decreasing when $v$ and $a$ have opposite signs
Deducing that speed is decreasing when $a < 0$, giving $2 < t < 4$

subparts.solution:
The speed of the particle is decreasing when $v$ and $a$ have opposite signs.
Now $v \ge 0$ for all $0 \le t \le 6$.
$\therefore$ the speed of the particle is decreasing when $a < 0$, which is when $2 < t < 4$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Speed is decreasing if and only if velocity and acceleration have opposite signs (i.e. $v(t) \cdot a(t) < 0$).
step_by_step: Recall the condition for decreasing speed: $v$ and $a$ have opposite signs.
Check the sign of $v(t)$ on $[0, 6]$; since $v(t) \ge 0$, we require $a(t) < 0$.
From the sign diagram of $a(t) = 3(t - 2)(t - 4)$, $a(t) < 0$ on the interval $(2, 4)$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Thinking speed decreases whenever acceleration is negative, which is only true when velocity is positive.
